VMT road type distributions by source type comparison of all data sets Figure 53 shows the road type distribution for vocations within source types. Across the four road types, each vocation’s distribution sums to 1. Keep in mind that FleetDNA and CE-CERT data did not observe vehicles driving on all road types within each vocation. For the combination-unit short-haul source type, FleetDNA contains food delivery, beverage delivery, local delivery, parcel delivery, and transfer truck vocations, while CE-CERT has 67 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. agricultural, cement mixers, construction, food distribution, line-haul, and municipal work vocations, and both data sets compose the drayage data. Beverage delivery and transfer trucks from FleetDNA and drayage trucks from both data sets display the strongest distribution in favor of urban other roads over urban freeways. Conversely, cement mixers, construction, and line- haul vehicles from CE-CERT and parcel delivery vehicles from FleetDNA all have stronger distributions in favor of urban freeways over urban other roads. Cement mixers, line-haul vehicles, and municipal work trucks from CE-CERT were the only vocations that we observe also driving on rural freeways at any noticeable rate. Food distribution from CE-CERT and food and local delivery from FleetDNA drove about equally on urban freeways and urban other roads. For single-unit short-haul vehicles, both data sets include towing data. FleetDNA contains food, parcel, linen, and warehouse delivery, as well as snow plows, while CE-CERT has beverage delivery, construction, local moving, freeway work, street sweeper, and utility vocations. Snow plows from FleetDNA and local moving trucks from CE-CERT both drive nearly all their miles on urban other roads. Single-unit linen and parcel delivery trucks from FleetDNA and towing trucks from both data sets in aggregate also drive far more of their miles on urban other roads than urban freeways. Interestingly, this relative proportion contrasts combination-unit parcel delivery trucks from FleetDNA, which spent many more miles on urban freeways, as described previously. Single-unit food and warehouse delivery trucks, as well as utility trucks, drove closer to even miles between the two urban road types, similar to food and local delivery vocations for combination-unit trucks. CE-CERT’s freeway work, beverage delivery, and street sweeper vocations were the only to drive notably on rural freeways; freeway work and street sweeper vehicles were also among the few vocations to drive many more miles on urban freeways than urban other roads. For the lower left chart in Figure 53, the darker shade of green for refuse trucks arises from CE- CERT data and the refuse pickup vocation from FleetDNA is a lighter green. CE-CERT refuse trucks spend more time on urban freeways compared to urban other roads and a very small amount of time on rural freeways.
